Prevention: The disease is transmitted by tools during field sanitary operations; before and after pruning each plant, disinfect tools with household bleach (1 part bleach to 9 parts water), even if the plants appear healthy
The disease is also transmitted by different insects from infected male flowers; remove the male bud as soon as the last female fingers emerge.
The bud is best removed by twisting off using the hand or a forked stick
It can be transmitted by infected plant parts (roots, trunk, bunch, fruit, peel, suckers or leaf material):
Do not move infested plant material to other farms
Sleeve bunches at an early stage before fingers emerge
Destroy all infected plant material by composting.
The composting should be performed away from the main growing area
Leave a fallow period of 6-12 months, ensuring that the disease dies out in the soil
Treat shoes with beach sloution before leaving an infested area
Monitoring: Symptoms may vary according to the strain of the bacterium, the mode of transmission and age of the plant.
If infection occurs via the roots:
Yellowing, wilting, necrosis and collapse of the oldest leaves at the petiole
Brown streaks and patches occur on the stem
Younger leaves develop pale green/white panels that become necrotic before dying.
Reddish-brown-black discoloration of the internal parts of the stem, exuding creamy bacterial ooze when cut
Fruit development stops and fingers may ripen prematurely and split, the inside of fruits blacken and rot
If transmitted by insects; flower buds become black and drop
Panama disease, Xanthomonas wilt, blood disease or bugtok
Act as soon as symptoms are seen in the plantation
Direct Control: Destroy any infected plants and all infected material from the plantation by cutting and composting or burning
If a whole area is infected, keep under quarantine, uproot plants and destroy properly
Moko disease cannot be control by chemicals
